title: Reconceiving the Tournament of Lawyers: Tracking, Seeding, and Information Control in the Internal Labor Markets of Elite Law Firms
pub: Virginia Law Review (84 Va. L. Rev. 1581)
author: David B. Wilkins · G. Mitu Gulati

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: The source does not directly assess whether stronger in-house buyers improve accountability while increasing professional-capture risks, nor does it endorse reciprocal duties or contextual regulation. Instead, it redirects attention to elite firms’ internal labour markets, arguing that professional socialisation, institutional rules and broader market factors—not buyer pressure alone—help explain lawyer conduct and organisational persistence.
qs: Through the internaliza- tion of professional norms relating to competence, client loyalty, and collegiality, most lawyers are predisposed to honor their pro- fessional commitments both to their clients and to each other.

The principal objection to tournament theory as a model of law firm growth is that it overlooks important factors that also plausibly contribute to law firm growth, including the demand for legal services, the supply of lawyers, and the restructuring of the legal services market through lateral hiring, mergers, and competition.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not address AI or selective deployment, so it cannot be said to accept or reject the cluster’s principal proposition. It does provide relevant pre-AI context: verification of discretionary junior work can require duplicative senior effort, and apprenticeship consumes substantial partner time, reinforcing the cluster’s concerns about verification capacity and professional development.
qs: Once again, monitoring these kinds of discretionary judgments effectively would require senior lawyers to duplicate much of the effort of their juniors.

More important, training work requires the firm to commit a substantial amount of uncompensated (or, at best, under- compensated) partner time because much of this valuable training can only be transmitted in the one-on-one, on-the-job context (e.g., being with the partner at a negotiation or at a client meeting).

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s focus on organisational mechanisms rather than firm size alone and materially extends its tournament and staffing analysis. It identifies a recruitment mechanism whereby elite firms, facing labour needs beyond the supply of committed partnership aspirants, recruit talented students with changeable preferences to enlarge the future partnership pool. This is a theoretical incentive, not evidence that firms successfully alter recruits’ ambitions.
qs: This fact is important because the labor needs of elite firms are likely to exceed the supply of students who have strong ex ante partnership intentions.

In addition, since the actual preferences of most law students are relatively weak and subject to change, firms have an incentive to recruit at least some talented students for whom the lure of partnership holds little current appeal, in the hopes of changing their minds and thereby increasing the talent pool from which they will eventually select partners.

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account that hourly billing reflects the difficulty and cost of measuring legal output, then materially extends it by showing that billed hours are a weak and manipulable proxy for associate quality and partnership potential. It does not address AI’s direct effect on firm profitability.
qs: The fact that law firms charge by input rather than by output suggests that output is too expensive to measure.” Simi- larly, firms pay their associates fixed salaries as opposed to paying piece-rate compensation by output.” Once again, this form of com- pensation suggests that output is difficult to measure.

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The source accepts partnership competition as important but materially develops the cluster’s proposition by replacing the standard rank-order tournament with an interdependent, multiround system of monitoring, differentiated training, sponsorship, forward-looking promotion and post-promotion competition. Its account directly strengthens the claim that partnership extends rather than ends competition while explaining unequal development access and information control.
qs: A plausible model of the internal labor markets of elite firms, therefore, must account for the fact that these institutions must re- solve two separate, albeit interrelated, problems: monitoring and training.

A growing num- ber of firms have specifically adopted a two-tiered partnership structure in which “junior” (salaried) partners compete to become “senior” (equity) partners.” Unlike the promotion-to-partner tour- nament, the sole criteria for winning this “partner” tournament is a junior partner’s demonstrated ability to bring in business and to as- sume primary responsibility on major matters for senior partners.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s governance thesis by offering a specific causal mechanism: restrictions on outside ownership and revenue sharing prevent aligned nonlawyer management, require lawyer self-management, and thereby sustain the promotion-to-partner tournament. It supports an ownership-and-decision-rights explanation rather than a capital-scarcity account, though it presents a theoretical argument rather than empirical evidence about AI-era adaptation.
qs: The restriction on sharing revenues with non-lawyers translates into a restriction on fully aligning the incentives of any potential non-lawyer manag- ers or directors with those of the revenue generating (and risk bearing) lawyers of the firm.

The need (in a large firm) to keep generating groups of lawyer-managers who will control and manage the firm, there- fore, creates the dynamic for a promotion-to-partner tournament as associates try to make it into this favored class.

st.t: Cravath model: Modern firms retain hollowed labels
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s historical account: early Cravath firms approximated a promotion tournament because specific client, labour and institutional conditions made the bargain plausible, not because the form was inherently optimal. It also stresses that the tournament never fully matched economic theory and notes that contemporary conditions differ substantially. However, the supplied excerpts do not independently develop the synthesis’s central modern claim that firms retain Cravath labels while abandoning core commitments.

kp.k: Historical framework, not an account of AI
kp.d: This 1998 article examines elite law firms’ internal labor markets, not AI. Wilkins and Gulati reject simple rank-order tournament theory while retaining competition for partnership as one component of a broader model incorporating monitoring, training, multiple incentives, tracking, seeding and information control. They expressly limit their critique of Galanter and Palay’s growth theory to its implications for understanding internal labor markets.
qs: The internal labor markets of elite law firms are not rank-order tournaments.
Because law firms remain partnerships, this structure still contains a tournament component.

kp.k: Evidence combines interviews, informal polling and published scholarship
kp.d: The authors ground their theoretical reconstruction in prior research on race and promotion, published studies, professional experience and observations of firms. They report that Wilkins conducted more than 150 in-depth interviews during the preceding eighteen months and that Gulati informally polled more than 100 lawyers. A separately reported informal poll found that only 33 of 183 current or former associates said they joined intending to make partner. These observations support the authors’ model rather than constituting a representative causal test of it.
qs: These observations are based on our respective work on, and in the case of Professor Gulati, work in elite firms.
only 33 out of 183 current or former associates at large, elite law firms stated that they joined their firms intending to make partner.

kp.k: Legal work remains difficult and expensive to monitor
kp.d: The authors defend the premise that supervising legal quality is costly. Hours are an imperfect proxy for effort and output; team production complicates attribution; polished writing does not establish thorough research; and short deadlines restrict checking. Detailed review requires scarce senior-lawyer time and displaces business development, even where some supervision can be billed to clients. This is an analysis of human legal work, not AI-output verification.
qs: With legal work, input is a weak measure of output.
The partner will not, however, be able easily to discern the associate’s effort and care in completing the assignment.
Time spent monitoring is time that cannot be spent developing new business.

kp.k: Training and paperwork create unequal career opportunities
kp.d: The article distinguishes developmental assignments that build judgment, client exposure and partner relationships from paperwork that generally builds more limited skills. Both kinds of work matter to production, but scarce training opportunities disproportionately determine access to senior associate and partnership roles. The distinction is analytical rather than absolute: the authors acknowledge that associates do some of both.
qs: Given this division of labor, every associate who wants to have a chance of winning the promotion-to-partner tournament needs to gain access to training work.
Of course, no associate does only paperwork.
Training, therefore, is an essential part of the bargain that Galanter and Palay posit between partners and associates in which the latter trade their labor for the chance to develop human capital.

kp.k: Paperwork economics encourage eventual associate departure
kp.d: The authors argue that paperwork associates receive less partner investment and experience relatively flat marginal productivity while salaries and benefits rise. Firms benefit from retaining them while their work remains profitable, but eventually have incentives to let them leave. Associates likewise face pressure to move before limited skill development and the appearance of partnership rejection damage their marketability. The article cites National Association for Law Placement figures reporting 43% departure from the first firm by year three and 66% by year five.
qs: After a certain number of years, the flatline of a pa- perwork associate’s marginal utility will drop below the marginal cost (measured in terms of the associate’s salary and benefits) of keeping that lawyer at the firm.
When that happens, the firm has every incentive to let the associate go.
reporting that 43% of all associates leave their first law firm by year three and 66% leave by year five

kp.k: Multiple incentives motivate associates beyond partnership
kp.d: The authors propose that above-market wages, reputational bonds and promised general training motivate many junior associates who do not intend to become partners. Losing a prestigious firm job can threaten both current earnings and the market value of educational and employment credentials. Their informal poll reported that 110 respondents out of 183, described in the source as 61%, primarily attributed effort to fear of losing high wages and sending a negative signal to future employers. The authors distinguish promises of training from its actual delivery.
qs: We suggest that firms rely on three additional motivational tools (beyond the chance for partnership) to either supplement or sup- plant the incentive effects of the tournament: high (above market) associate wages, associate reputational bonds, and the promise of general (as opposed to firm-specific) training.
The less credible a firm’s partnership prom- ises, the more it is likely to rely on high wages or promises of pro- viding valuable external signals.

kp.d: The proposed multiround model describes informal training and paperwork tracks beneath formally uniform associate classifications. Early success leads to preferential assignments, stronger mentoring relationships and greater protection when mistakes occur. This concentrates training investment in lawyers firms hope to retain, strengthens their partnership ambitions and encourages others to depart. Movement between tracks remains possible, but the authors expect early access to training to advantage eventual winners.
qs: As a formal matter, firms maintain few distinctions between as- sociates in a given class.
This formal uniformity, however, masks fundamental differences between the experiences and opportuni- ties of particular associates.
Associates who continue to get good work are more likely to be happy and to stay at the firm.

kp.k: Seeding rewards credentials before demonstrated legal performance
kp.d: Some recruits receive immediate access to developmental work because of law-school prestige, grades, law review membership or clerkships. The authors argue that these indicators only loosely predict actual lawyering ability, but provide visible and rankable signals to clients and future recruits. Seeding therefore serves both retention and external reputation, rather than simply identifying the most skilled lawyers.
qs: Instead, some as- sociates are “seeded” directly onto the training track.
These easily observable signals only loosely correlate with actual lawyering skills.
As a result, law firm seeding is based on limited and narrow information—i.e., on signals that do not necessarily have a high correlation with skills.

kp.k: Team production limits the usefulness of universal competition
kp.d: Because firms depend on cooperation under client deadlines, a competition involving every associate could induce information withholding, sabotage and struggles over training. The authors observe relatively little visible junior-associate sabotage and interpret this as inconsistent with a universal rank-order tournament. Restricting intense partnership competition to a smaller pool, often working in separate arenas, helps reconcile cooperation with competitive incentives.
qs: A firm structured entirely as a tournament would not be an envi- ronment that fostered cooperation simply because one’s success in the standard tournament is a direct function of others not per- forming as well.
Large law firms, however, do not appear to be characterized by high levels of employee sabotage.

kp.k: Partner interests make promotion a political process
kp.d: Partners are participants as well as judges: they compete over compensation, leadership and continued membership. Individual partners may underinvest in broadly shared training while favoring protégés who benefit their own practices or offer future support. Associates consequently seek powerful sponsors rather than simply accepting whichever work best serves the firm. The authors treat relational capital as central to both opportunity allocation and promotion.
qs: This image of partners as neutral de- cisionmakers fails to capture the fact that partners are players as well as judges.
Training is costly to individual partners—time spent training is time that the partner cannot spend either produc- ing revenue or consuming leisure.
Given these realities, we should expect tournament winners to be selected as much on the basis of politics as on firm efficiency.

kp.k: Partnership predicts future contribution rather than rewarding past output
kp.d: The authors argue that partnership requires an absolute threshold of human and relational capital, anticipated business demand and confidence in future contribution—not merely superior associate performance. Partners must attract business and assume responsibilities that associates have rarely tested. Citing O’Flaherty and Siow’s study of large New York firms, they report that associate performance is not especially informative about partner performance. Business-cycle risk therefore falls on associates even where their work is excellent.
qs: The most important work done by today’s large law firm partners is bringing in business.
Associates do virtually no rainmaking.
Thus, the fundamental issue with respect to both the indi- vidual candidate and the firm’s needs is one of prediction, not reward.
the promotion structure is one in which the risk of fluctuations in the external market is borne by the associates and not the firm.

kp.k: The strongest tournament operates among senior associates
kp.d: Competition for partnership becomes the principal incentive among trained senior associates approaching the decision. They have accumulated firm-specific and relational capital, face diminishing lateral prospects and compete for limited positions. The article reports contemporary partnership rates of six to ten percent in many firms and cites a 1998 report that 9.7% of associates entering the eight highest-grossing New York firms from 1985 to 1987 became partners at those same firms. These historical figures are not current-market estimates.
qs: The real tournament, therefore, only begins when a lawyer be- comes a senior associate.
Today, these rates hover between six and ten percent in many firms.
For example, of the associates who entered the eight highest grossing New York firms from 1985 to 1987, 9.7% became partners at that same firm.

kp.k: Partnership introduces further rounds rather than secure tenure
kp.d: The article identifies two-tier partnerships and compensation ladders as mechanisms for inducing continued effort after initial promotion. Salaried partners may compete for equity, while equity partners compete for higher compensation and leadership. Revenue generation is important, but attributing client origination and contribution remains contentious. The authors describe these arrangements as additional tournament-like rounds supplemented by wages and reputation, not standard rank-order tournaments.
qs: A growing num- ber of firms have specifically adopted a two-tiered partnership structure in which “junior” (salaried) partners compete to become “senior” (equity) partners.
The argument that “eat-what-you-kill” compensa- tion systems demonstrate that monitoring and evaluating partners is easy ignores the tremendous difficulty of determining who “killed” what.

kp.k: Information control sustains effort and conceals unequal opportunities
kp.d: The authors argue that opaque promotion criteria encourage senior associates to work across all dimensions rather than optimize disclosed metrics, coast when ahead or leave when behind. For juniors, selective disclosure reassures favored associates while keeping others uncertain about their actual prospects. This opacity also enables opportunism, including obscuring compensation differences or invoking business conditions strategically. The authors doubt that such information management provides a stable solution as disclosure increases.
qs: Instead, firms pursue a “black box” approach in which associates are provided only a vague idea about the criteria for making partner and almost no in- formation about how these criteria are applied in particular cases.

Keeping associates uncertain about what weights are given to the different factors (or even about precisely what those factors are) induces them to work hard on everything and not just on the acquisition of signals.
For these reasons, we doubt that the tournament we describe constitutes a stable solution to the problem firms face in motivating and monitoring lawyers in this age of information and opportun- ism.

kp.k: Ownership restrictions and professional ideology reinforce inherited structures
kp.d: The authors explain continued reliance on the Cravath-derived partnership model through path dependence, professional values and restrictions on nonlawyer ownership and fee-sharing, citing the 1997 Model Rule 5.4 and contemporary restrictions. In their account, these constraints limit public share ownership and fully aligned outside management, reinforcing the need to develop lawyer-managers internally. This is a historical institutional argument, not a description of subsequent regulatory reforms.
qs: As Robert Nelson has documented, institu- tional structures in law firms are frequently viewed as closely linked to professional values.
As a result, law firms cannot sell shares to the public or adopt many of the other practices of a typi- cal corporation.
That inability to align incentives, in turn, means that the lawyers at the firm have to manage the firm themselves.

kp.k: Unequal opportunities can systematically disadvantage particular groups
kp.d: Drawing on their earlier research, the authors argue that average black associates face greater difficulty reaching the training track than average white associates. They also argue that long-hours norms and especially unpredictable emergency availability may disadvantage women with family responsibilities. These are distributional implications of assignment allocation, subjective evaluation and work organization, not findings about AI or claims that every associate has the same experience.
qs: Average black lawyers, for example, are likely to find it more difficult to get themselves on the training track than average white lawyers.

However, our conversations with women lawyers at large firms suggest that over and above the long hours, what dis- proportionately affects women with family responsibilities is the unpredictability of the work.

kp.k: Analysis must integrate skills, signals and relationships
kp.d: The article concludes that human-capital accounts alone miss why firms favor certain credentials, how sponsors shape careers and why promotion protects future interests. It recommends combining economic analysis with signaling, relational capital and cultural or political explanations. The authors present firms as institutionally unsettled under pressures including lateral hiring, multitier partnerships, contract lawyers, demanding clients and global competition, rather than predicting a single settled organizational outcome.
qs: Signaling theory and relational capital must therefore be a part of any comprehensive examination of the large law firm as an economic institution.
Creating analytic models that synthesize different methodologies is an essential step if we are to understand the future evolution of the large law firm.

It is clear that these institutions are far from equilibrium in their attempt to create institutional structures that can respond to the demands of the future while holding onto the best of their past.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: No AI-related claims or predictions are made in this source.
pts.d: Wilkins and Gulati analyse elite law firms’ internal labour markets, including associate incentives, training, tracking, seeding, partnership selection and information control. The article does not discuss artificial intelligence or attribute changes in legal services to AI. It is a legal-profession source rather than a cross-domain source; its organisational claims therefore should not be recast as claims about AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: No evidence is offered about AI’s effects.
pts.d: The authors support their non-AI organisational analysis with published scholarship, observations, professional experience and interviews. These materials are not evidence of AI adoption, performance or effects on legal work.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: There is no AI-related timeframe or conditional prediction.
pts.d: Published in 1998, the article addresses contemporary elite firms and historical changes in their organisation. Its discussion of future institutional adaptation does not identify AI as a cause or condition.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No group is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: The source discusses elite firms, junior and senior associates, partners, recruits and clients, including differential career opportunities for Black lawyers and women. These are effects attributed to organisational practices and market conditions, not to AI.
